newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Durables, more supply.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Durables, more supply.

text.p: The U.S. credit market will turn its attention to the August durable goods report on Wednesday morning before gearing up for the Treasury's five-year note sale in the afternoon.
The content of the durable goods report -- a notoriously volatile indicator -- and the market's reaction to the number should help dictate the five-year note's reception, analysts predicted.

"If durables come in below consensus I think it will be a positive and we should be able to hang on to Wednesday's gains and attract some demand for the five-year notes," said John Canavan, treasury market analyst at Stone & McCarthy Research Associates.
"Any unexpected strength in the durables could make things a little more hairy and it becomes more of a wait-and-see issue for the five-year," he added.
Economists surveyed by Reuters were calling for a 0.1 percent decline in durable goods orders for August and a 0.7 percent drop excluding the defense sector.
This compares to a strong 1.7 percent overall advance in July and a 3.6 percent spike ex-defense.

On Wednesday, a strong two-year note auction and reported central bank buying helped push Treasuries substantially higher. The benchmark 6.75 percent two-year note was up 21/32 at 97-22/32 to yield 6.93 percent in late dealings.
Analysts said the key question for the five-year notes was whether the foreign interest generated by Wednesday's two-year sale would continue.
In addition to the durables report, jobless claims for the week ended September 21 could also generate some interest in early trade, particularly if they show a sizable decline.
"Jobless claims have been very low and that has been a key source of concern as far as inflation goes," said Dan Seto,
Economists surveyed by Reuters are expecting only a modest decline in claims to 328,000 from 329,000 in the prior week.

In the final analysis however, market analysts said that Thursday's numbers should shed little light on the inflation picture -- the focus of Treasuries in the aftermath of the Federal Reserve's steady policy decision on Tuesday.
The federal funds rate is expected to open between 5-1/4 and 5-3/8 percent on Thursday.
